etymology: Latin secundus (second) plus the verbal noun of call. The second-order calling: not the call to Christ Himself but the call to a particular work in His service.
biblical_def: Secondary calling is the believer's call to a particular work in the world — the trade, craft, post, or station that the saint occupies under the Lord. The Reformers distinguished it from the primary calling (the call to Christ Himself): both are real, both come from God, and both are to be honored.
webster_summary: (Theological.) The believer's second-order calling to a particular work, station, or vocation under the Lord.
webster_full: Calling in Webster: “profession or trade; vocation; the divine summons to special work.”

Reformation theology distinguishes the two callings: the primary calling is to Christ (God calls each saint personally to Himself); the secondary calling is to a particular work or station in this world. Both come from God; the second is no less holy for being also vocational.
scriptures: But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called.
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often divides life into ‘sacred’ and ‘secular’; the Reformers saw the saint's daily work as part of his calling to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 3:23 dissolves the sacred-secular split: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord. Plumbing, teaching, soldiering, mothering, programming — each becomes service to Christ when received as secondary calling.

Recover this and the Marine's post, the mother's kitchen, the farmer's field, the programmer's desk all become liturgy. Daily work is not what one does to fund worship; it is part of worship, when received as call.
roots_summary: Greek klēsis (calling) and Hebrew melakah (work) underlie the concept.
roots_lines: Greek klēsis — calling, invitation; behind vocation in Eph 4:1.
Hebrew melakah — work, occupation, business; the appointed labor of the saint.
usage: The Marine's post is a calling; so is the mother's kitchen.
Daily work is part of worship when received as call.
Walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called — both callings, both honored.

etymology: Latin professio, the public declaration; one's declared trade or faith.
biblical_def: Profession in Scripture is what one publicly declares — both the trade by which one earns and the faith by which one lives. Hebrews calls believers to hold fast our profession; Paul appeals to Timothy's good profession before many witnesses. The two senses are not unrelated: the household's profession of faith shapes the household's practice of trade.
webster_summary: Open declaration; public avowal; that which is professed; one's declared trade or faith.
webster_full: PROFESSION, n. The act of avowing or acknowledging openly; the declaration of one's faith or trade. The business which one professes to understand and to follow.

Hebrews uses homologia (profession, confession) of faith; Paul applies the same word to Christ's good confession before Pilate (1 Tim 6:13). The household's daily trade and the household's public faith share the verb.
scriptures: Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession.
corruption_summary: Modern usage uses ‘profession’ for trade only; Scripture preserves both the trade and the public faith-declaration in one word.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews' profession in 4:14 and 10:23 is faith made public — the saint's declared loyalty held fast through trial. The vocational profession is its weekday twin: the saint's declared craft practiced with integrity.
Recover both senses and the household's identity sharpens. The Christian carpenter's profession is two: he is a Christian, he is a carpenter. Both are professed; both are practiced.
roots_summary: Greek homologia (same-word, agreement, confession) is the New Testament term.
roots_lines: Greek homologia — profession, confession; literally ‘same-word’, agreement spoken aloud.
Note: same root as homologeō, to confess; Romans 10:9's ‘confess with thy mouth’.
usage: Hold fast our profession — that is faith held public.
The household's trade and the household's faith share one word.
Christ's good confession before Pilate stands as the template.

etymology: Old English cræft (skill, strength); the learned trade by which one shapes material into useful or beautiful things.
biblical_def: Craft is the learned trade — the manual skill by which one shapes wood, metal, cloth, or stone into useful or beautiful things. Scripture honors the craftsman: Bezalel was filled with the Spirit of God for craft work on the tabernacle (Ex 31:3); Christ Himself was a tekton, the carpenter of Nazareth; Paul made tents to support his ministry.
webster_summary: An art; a manual occupation requiring skill; a trade learned by apprenticeship and practice.
webster_full: CRAFT, n. Art; ability; dexterity; skill in a particular manual occupation. Manual art; trade; employment that requires manual skill.

Ex 31:1-5 records the first Spirit-anointing in Scripture: not a prophet or king but a craftsman, Bezalel, filled with the Spirit of God in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship.
scriptures: And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship.
Them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer.
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon?
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
corruption_summary: Modern industrial culture has marginalized the craftsman; Scripture treats craft as Spirit-filled service worthy of named honor.
corruption_paragraphs: Bezalel and Aholiab (Ex 31, 35) are named at length and described as filled with the Spirit specifically for craft. The Spirit's first recorded indwelling is for the trade of working wood, metal, and cloth for God's house.

Industrial production has dignity, but craft has weight. The Christian craftsman — carpenter, mason, smith, weaver, cook, programmer at the artisanal end — serves God in the shape of his hands. Recover the dignity of craft and the household has more to honor in its breadwinners.
roots_summary: Greek tektōn (craftsman, builder) and Hebrew melakah (work, craft) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Greek tektōn — craftsman, builder, carpenter; the title applied to Joseph and to Christ Himself (Mt 13:55; Mk 6:3).
Hebrew melakah — work, craft, occupation; the labor of Bezalel and Aholiab (Ex 35:35).
usage: Christ was a tekton; the trade is no shame.
Bezalel's anointing was Spirit-filled craft, not Spirit-filled rhetoric.
The household honors the breadwinner's shaped hands.

etymology: Old English hūsbonda (master of the house); the householder's discipline of cultivating land and raising livestock.
biblical_def: Husbandry is the patient cultivation of land and livestock — the discipline by which the householder turns soil and herd into food and provision. Scripture is full of husbandry vocabulary: God Himself is called the husbandman in John 15; Paul calls the church God's husbandry; the noble work of farming is treated as priestly stewardship of creation.
webster_summary: The business of a farmer, comprehending agriculture or tillage of the ground, the raising and feeding of cattle, and the management of farm produce.
webster_full: HUSBANDRY, n. The business of a farmer; the cultivation of the ground; the rearing of livestock; thrift; frugal and prudent management.
Webster's second sense — thrift, prudent management — preserves the householder's broader stewardship: not just farming, but the patient management of the household's resources, time, and people.
scriptures: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
The husbandman that laboureth must be first partaker of the fruits.
corruption_summary: Industrial food systems hide husbandry from most households; Scripture treats it as the householder's archetypal work.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 2:15 establishes the original calling before the Fall: dress and keep the garden. Husbandry is not a curse-task; it is the dignified, pre-Fall work of the householder. The curse made it sweat-soaked, not less holy.

Recover husbandry in any form — a garden, chickens, even a tended houseplant — and the household reconnects with the rhythm of seed, seasons, and patient growth that Scripture assumes its readers know. The lessons embedded in farming are catechism.
roots_summary: Greek geōrgos (farmer, husbandman) is the New Testament term.
roots_lines: Greek geōrgos — husbandman, farmer (Jn 15:1; 2 Tim 2:6).
Note: cognate with geōrgia (farming); ‘George’ means farmer.
usage: God is the husbandman; the church is His husbandry.
Garden, herd, household — husbandry covers them all.
Recover husbandry in any form; the lessons are catechism.

etymology: Old English tilian (to strive, cultivate); the patient breaking and turning of soil before the seed.
biblical_def: Tilling is the patient labor of breaking up the ground before any seed is sown — the unglamorous first work that makes everything else possible. Hosea calls Israel to break up your fallow ground; Christ's parable of the four soils assumes that the difference between fruit and barrenness lies first in what was done to the soil.
webster_summary: The act of tilling; cultivation of the soil by plowing, harrowing, and similar work.
webster_full: TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice, or art of preparing land for seed, and keeping the ground in a proper state for the growth of crops.

Hosea 10:12 makes tillage spiritual: break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you. The unbroken heart, like the unbroken field, will not receive seed.
scriptures: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground.
Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.
He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity wants harvest without the unglamorous first labor of tilling; Scripture insists the soil must be broken before the seed is sown.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 10:12 puts the order: break up your fallow ground first; then sow; then reap. Cut any step and the harvest fails. Many discipleship efforts begin with sowing on hard ground and wonder why nothing grows.

The household's tilling is the slow daily work of confession, prayer, restored relationships, named sins, refused habits. The unspectacular labor that softens the soil. Tilling done, sowing has a chance.
roots_summary: Hebrew avad (to till, work, serve) underlies the verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew avad — to work, serve, till; the verb at Genesis 2:15 of Adam tilling the garden.
Note: same verb behind worship as service; tillage and worship share a root.
usage: Break up your fallow ground; that is the first labor.
Tilling done, sowing has a chance.
Many sow on hard hearts and wonder why nothing grows.

etymology: Old English teōtha (tenth) plus pattern. The biblical practice of returning the tenth as recognition that the whole belongs to God.
biblical_def: The tithing pattern is the biblical practice of giving back to God the tenth of one's increase. Older than Moses (Abram tithed to Melchizedek, Gen 14:20), embedded in the Mosaic law (Lev 27:30; Deut 14:22), and reaffirmed by Christ (Mt 23:23) without abolishing the spirit. The tithe is not the upper limit of giving; it is the beginning, the proportion that confesses the whole belongs to God.
webster_summary: The biblical practice of giving the tenth part of one's increase to God.
webster_full: Webster: tithe — “the tenth part of any thing.”

Three Old Testament tithes: the Levitical tithe (annual, for the Levites, Num 18); the festival tithe (annual, for celebration in Jerusalem, Deut 14:22-26); the third-year tithe (every third year, for the poor, Levite, stranger, widow, Deut 14:28-29). The full Mosaic system was therefore more than 10% in any given year.
scriptures: And he gave him tithes of all.
And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD's: it is holy unto the LORD.
Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven.
Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin... these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity treats the tithe as either obsolete or as the upper limit; Scripture treats it as the floor of faithful giving.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ in Matthew 23:23 commends the Pharisees' meticulous tithing — these ought ye to have done — while rebuking their neglect of weightier matters. He does not abolish the practice; He insists the practice not crowd out justice, mercy, and faith.

The household's tithing pattern is its first weekly confession that the whole income belongs to the LORD. Beyond the tithe, generosity flows; below the tithe, even basic stewardship has not been claimed. Malachi 3:10 still stands as invitation: prove me now herewith.
roots_summary: Hebrew maaser (tenth) and Greek dekatos (tenth) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Hebrew maaser — the tenth part; the tithe.
Greek dekatos — tenth; behind dekatoo (to tithe) of Heb 7:6,9.
usage: The tithe is the floor of giving, not the ceiling.
Prove me now herewith — Malachi's invitation still stands.
These ought ye to have done; Christ commended the practice.

etymology: Old French toiler (to dispute, struggle); the painful labor that exhausts the body.
biblical_def: Toil is the painful labor that exhausts the body — the post-Fall texture of work introduced in Genesis 3:17-19: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it. Solomon names vanity and vexation of spirit as the toil of the man without God; Paul redeems toil by working night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you.
webster_summary: Labor with pain and fatigue; that which exhausts the strength.
webster_full: TOIL, n. Labor with pain and fatigue; severe exertion; that which exhausts the body, and especially that which is unrelieved by pleasure.
Distinguished from work itself: work was given pre-Fall (Gen 2:15); toil is work's post-Fall texture (Gen 3:17-19) — the same labor, now sweat-soaked and resisted by thorns.
scriptures: Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life.
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.
For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun?
For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel.
corruption_summary: Modern wellness culture treats toil as suspect; Scripture treats it as honorable post-Fall work, redeemed by Christ's finished labor.
corruption_paragraphs: The Fall did not abolish work; it cursed work's soil. Adam still tilled, but now the ground fought back. Toil is therefore inevitable in this age — the saint who expects frictionless labor under the sun has missed Genesis 3.

Christ's cross redeems toil. The new heavens and new earth will end it. Until then, the saint toils as worship, knowing that your labour is not in vain in the Lord (1 Cor 15:58). The toil is real; the meaning is final.
roots_summary: Greek kopiaō (to toil) and Hebrew amal (laborious toil) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Greek kopiaō — to toil, work to weariness; Paul's standard verb for ministry labor.
Hebrew amal — laborious toil, sorrow; one of Ecclesiastes' key vocabulary words.
usage: Toil is work's post-Fall texture, not work's nature.
Your labor is not in vain in the Lord — the redemption-word.
The Marine knows: real work soaks the shirt.

etymology: Old French vigne (vine) plus Old English geard (yard) and cypa (keeper). The patient husbandman of grapes.
biblical_def: The vineyard keeper is the patient husbandman of grapes — pruner, watcher, harvester. Scripture is dense with vineyard imagery: Israel as the LORD's vineyard (Isa 5:1-7), Christ as the true vine (Jn 15:1), the Father as the vinedresser, the saints as branches. The vineyard keeper's art — pruning, watching, defending — is the great picture of pastoral work.
webster_summary: (Composite.) One who tends a vineyard; a vinedresser; the husbandman of grapes.
webster_full: Webster: vinedresser — “a husbandman or tender of vines.”

Old Testament vineyard imagery climaxes in the Song of the Vineyard (Isa 5:1-7), where Israel is the LORD's carefully tended vineyard that produced wild grapes. New Testament imagery climaxes in John 15: Christ is the true vine, the Father the vinedresser, the saints the branches.
scriptures: Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill.
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often skips the pruning verses; the vineyard keeper's art includes deliberate cutting away, even of fruitful branches.
corruption_paragraphs: John 15:2 is uncomfortable: every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it. The vinedresser cuts even the fruitful branch — not to punish, but to multiply fruit. Pruning is the ordinary love of the Father for the bearing branch.

The pastor who refuses to prune is no vineyard keeper. The household that resists pruning will not multiply. Recover the vinedresser image and the difficult seasons of the saint's life take on different meaning: the Father is keeping the vineyard.
roots_summary: Greek geōrgos (farmer) and Hebrew kerem (vineyard) underlie the picture.
roots_lines: Greek geōrgos — husbandman, farmer; here applied to the Father in John 15:1.
Hebrew kerem — vineyard; one of Israel's defining national crops.
usage: The Father is the vinedresser; trust His shears.
Pruning is the ordinary love of the Father for the bearing branch.
The pastor who refuses to prune is no vineyard keeper.

etymology: Old French waitier (to watch, attend); originally any servant who waited at table; in modern usage, the table-server.
biblical_def: A waiter in Scripture is a servant who waits at table or attends a master — an honorable role, not a humble one. The word covers both the literal table-server (Acts 6:2: serve tables) and the saint who waits on the Lord (Ps 27:14: wait on the LORD). Both are the same posture: ready, attentive, deferring to the master.
webster_summary: One who waits; a personal attendant; one who serves at table.
webster_full: WAITER, n. One who waits; one in attendance; an attendant; a servant in attendance, particularly at table.
The Greek diakoneō (to wait at table, to serve) gave the church deacon. The very office that organizes the church's service was named after waiting at table.
scriptures: It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.
And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink?
Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength.
corruption_summary: Modern culture treats waiting on tables as low-status work; Scripture honors it enough to name the church's service-office after it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek diakonos (deacon) literally means ‘table-waiter’. The early church organized its diaconate around literal waiting at the widows' tables (Acts 6:1-6). The first deacons were waiters.

The household's waiter at the family table — the one who serves the meal — is rehearsing the deacon's office. Christ Himself, on the night He was betrayed, girded Himself with a towel and washed feet. The Master waited; the saints follow.
roots_summary: Greek diakoneō (to wait at table, serve) underlies the diaconate.
roots_lines: Greek diakoneō — to wait at table, to serve; root of diakonos (deacon).
Hebrew qavah — to wait, hope, expect; the verb behind ‘wait on the LORD’.
usage: Waiter is honorable; the deacon's office is named after it.
Wait on the LORD — the same posture as waiting at His table.
Christ girded Himself with a towel; the Master waited.

etymology: Latin instaurare (to set up) plus Old English corn (grain). The accumulated provision laid up against future need.
biblical_def: A store of grain is the accumulated provision laid up against future need. Joseph in Egypt stored grain for seven years against the seven of famine and saved many lives. The ant of Proverbs 6 stores in summer for winter. Christ's parable of the foolish farmer warns of storing grain without storing toward God. The biblical pattern is forethought without idolatry.
webster_summary: (Composite.) Stored grain; the accumulated harvest laid up against future need.
webster_full: Webster: store — “a quantity laid up for future use; supply; provision.”
Two storage scenes anchor the biblical concept: Joseph's wise storage (Gen 41:48) and the foolish farmer's self-centered storage (Lk 12:18). One saves a nation; one loses a soul.
scriptures: He gathered up all the food of the seven years, which were in the land of Egypt, and laid up the food in the cities.
Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
corruption_summary: Modern wealth-management culture confuses biblical foresight with biblical hoarding; Christ's parable distinguishes them sharply.
corruption_paragraphs: Joseph stored grain for a coming famine and a watching nation; he was provident. The rich fool stored grain so he could say to his soul, take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry; he was an idolater. Same act, opposite hearts.

The household's savings is therefore not a moral neutral. Stored toward future provision and generosity, it is wisdom; stored toward self-secured comfort, it competes with God. The test question: am I rich toward God?
roots_summary: Hebrew otzar (storehouse, treasure) is the foundational term.
roots_lines: Hebrew otzar — treasury, storehouse; the place of accumulated provision (Mal 3:10).
Note: same word for both grain stores and royal treasuries.
usage: Joseph stored toward famine and a watching nation; the rich fool stored toward self.
Same act, opposite hearts.
Am I rich toward God? — the diagnostic question.

etymology: Greek thēsauros (storehouse, treasure); the accumulated wealth or stored value, whether material or moral.
biblical_def: Treasure store is the accumulated wealth or stored value — material or moral — that one has laid up. Christ's sharpest teaching on it: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth... but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. The store is real; the question is where it is laid up. The heart, He says, follows the store.
webster_summary: An accumulated stock of valuables, money, or moral worth; that which is treasured up.
webster_full: Greek thēsauros covers both the storehouse itself and the treasure stored in it; the same word translated treasure in Mt 6:19 and storehouse in some contexts.
Christ's logic in Matthew 6 runs: where the treasure is, there the heart will be. The store determines the affection, not the other way around. Lay it up rightly, and the heart follows.
scriptures: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal.
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often quotes ‘where your treasure is, there your heart will be’ as descriptive; Christ uses it as prescriptive — build the store rightly, and the heart will move.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 6:21 is often misread: I will follow my heart and the treasure will go where my heart is. Christ teaches the opposite: choose where to lay up the store, and the heart will follow it. The order is treasure-then-heart, not heart-then-treasure.
Practically: the household's budget is its discipling document. Where the money goes, the affections will follow. Move the store; move the heart.
roots_summary: Greek thēsauros covers both store and stored value.
roots_lines: Greek thēsauros — storehouse, treasure; same word for the place and the contents.
Note: behind English thesaurus (a store of words).
usage: Build the store rightly; the heart will follow.
The household's budget is its discipling document.
Where the treasure is, there the heart will be — that is prescription, not description.

etymology: Italian artigiano, from Latin ars (skill); the practitioner of a trained skilled trade.
biblical_def: An artisan is the practitioner of a trained, skilled trade — the carpenter, mason, smith, weaver, embroiderer. Scripture honors them by name: Bezalel and Aholiab on the tabernacle, Hiram on the temple, Christ Himself the carpenter of Nazareth. The kingdom uses artisans; the church should not be ashamed of them.
webster_summary: One who professes and practices an art in which manual skill is required; a handicraftsman; a mechanic.
webster_full: ARTISAN, n. One who professes and practices some art in which manual labor is requisite, as a painter, sculptor, carpenter, or weaver; a handicraftsman.
1 Kings 7:13-14 names Hiram of Tyre as filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass. The temple was built with named artisans; their craft is preserved in Scripture.
scriptures: And Moses said unto the children of Israel, See, the LORD hath called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri.
He was a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning.
For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana.
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?
corruption_summary: Modern professional culture devalues manual artisan work; Scripture names the artisans by name and honors their Spirit-given skill.
corruption_paragraphs: Bezalel, Aholiab, Hiram — Scripture names artisans by name. The tabernacle and temple were built by men whose craft is preserved in the inspired record. The kingdom does not function without them.

Recover the dignity of the artisan and the church begins to honor again what God always honored. The carpenter, the welder, the seamstress, the cook, the artisanal programmer — each is a candidate for the Bezalel anointing of skilled work for the kingdom.
roots_summary: Greek tektōn (craftsman) and Hebrew charash (artisan, engraver) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Greek tektōn — craftsman; the title of Joseph and of Christ.
Hebrew charash — artisan, engraver, smith; one who shapes hard material with skill.
usage: Bezalel was Spirit-anointed for craft, not for rhetoric.
Christ was an artisan; the trade is no shame.
The kingdom honors the named artisan.

etymology: Old English weorc (work) plus man plus scipe (state of being). The quality of work done by a workman.
biblical_def: Workmanship is the visible quality of work done by a workman — what the work shows about the worker. Paul calls the church God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works. The saint is the work; the saint also does the work. Both senses run together: God's workmanship producing more workmanship.
webster_summary: The art or skill of a workman; the work done; the quality of execution.
webster_full: WORKMANSHIP, n. The art or skill of a workman; the manner of executing or producing any work; the quality of work done.
Greek poiēma (Eph 2:10) is the word translated workmanship: literally that which is made; behind English poem. The saint is God's poem, His handcrafted creation.
scriptures: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
And in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber, to work in all manner of workmanship.
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
corruption_summary: Modern culture often treats output as quantity; Scripture treats workmanship as quality — the visible mark the workman leaves on his work.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew workmanship of Bezalel (Ex 31:5) and the Greek workmanship of Ephesians 2:10 share a focus: the work bears the workman's mark. The tabernacle bore Bezalel's; the saint bears God's.

Recover this and daily work shifts. The household, workplace, and church begin to ask: what does this work say about its worker? The Christian craftsman's answer is supposed to be different from the world's — not by perfection, but by an unmistakable signature of care, integrity, and dignity.
roots_summary: Greek poiēma and Hebrew maaseh both name the made thing.
roots_lines: Greek poiēma — that which is made, workmanship, poem; the saint as God's crafted work (Eph 2:10).
Hebrew maaseh — work, deed, labor, accomplishment; the heavens are His workmanship (Ps 19:1).
usage: The saint is God's poem; the trade speaks of its Worker.
The work bears the workman's mark; what does yours say?
Bezalel's workmanship and the saint's share a Greek root.

etymology: Latin dignitas (worth, rank) plus Old English weorc. The recognized worth of honest labor as service to God.
biblical_def: The dignity of work is the recognized worth of honest labor as service to God. Genesis 2:15 establishes work pre-Fall as the dignified vocation of the man God placed in His garden. Paul commands those that work with quietness, and eat their own bread (2 Thess 3:12) and condemns idleness. Honest work, however humble, is honorable in the kingdom.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The recognized worth and honor of honest labor as service to God and neighbor.
webster_full: Webster: dignity — “true honor; nobleness or elevation of mind, consisting in a high sense of propriety, truth, and justice.”

Applied to work: the New Testament refuses to despise honest labor of any kind. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3); Christ was a carpenter (Mk 6:3); the deaconess Phoebe was a prostatis, a working patroness. None of this is condescension; all of it is honor.
scriptures: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
And to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often whispers a hierarchy — ministry > everything else — that the New Testament does not authorize.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul commanded the Thessalonians to work with their own hands. Not poetry: hands. The dignity of work in the New Testament covers the manual, the menial, the technical, and the elevated alike. The hierarchy is moral, not categorical: a faithful trash collector outranks an unfaithful pastor.

Recover this and the household stops apologizing for honest labor. The mother at the laundry, the father at the lathe, the teenager at the fast-food register — each is doing dignified work when done as to the Lord.
roots_summary: Greek ergazomai (to work) and Hebrew avad (to work, serve) cover the New Testament work-dignity vocabulary.
roots_lines: Greek ergazomai — to work, labor; the verb of 1 Thess 4:11 and 2 Thess 3:10.
Hebrew avad — to work, serve; same word for tilling soil and serving God.
usage: Work with your own hands — Paul did not blush.
A faithful trash collector outranks an unfaithful pastor.
The hierarchy is moral, not categorical.

etymology: Old English siex plus dæg. The biblical pattern: six days of labor, one of rest, repeated indefinitely.
biblical_def: Six-day work is the biblical labor pattern: six days of work followed by one of rest, week after week. The pattern is older than Sinai (Gen 2:2-3) and embedded in the Fourth Commandment: six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: but the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God. The rhythm shapes the household, the body, and the soul.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The biblical labor pattern of six days' work followed by one day of rest.
webster_full: Genesis 2:2-3 establishes the pattern at creation: God worked six days and rested the seventh; Israel was commanded to imitate it (Ex 20:9-11; Ex 34:21). The pattern long predates and outlasts the specific Sabbath legislation.
Christianity has shifted the rest-day to Sunday (the Lord's day, Rev 1:10) but preserves the rhythm. Six and one. The household ignores it at its peril.
scriptures: Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work.
But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God.
Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest.
And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
corruption_summary: Modern culture either overworks (no rest) or underworks (no labor); Scripture commands both halves of the rhythm.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 20:9 is often forgotten by those who quote 20:10: six days shalt thou labour. The Sabbath assumes the six. The household that does not work the six has no Sabbath to enter; the household that does not rest the seventh has not yet learned dependence on God.

Recover the rhythm and life simplifies. Six days of intentional labor — deep, focused, varied. One day of rest. Stop apologizing for either half. The body, the marriage, and the work all benefit from the cadence God built into creation.
roots_summary: Hebrew shesheth (six) plus the work-vocabulary already covered.
roots_lines: Hebrew shesheth — six; the cardinal number of the labor-days.
Note: the seventh-day Sabbath rest is grounded in creation (Gen 2:2-3), not first introduced at Sinai — pre-Fall, pre-law.
usage: Six days of work; one of rest. Both halves required.
The Sabbath assumes the six; the work assumes the rest.
Stop apologizing for either half.

etymology: Hebrew shabbat (cease, rest) joined with the English work-rest rhythm.
biblical_def: The Sabbath is the seventh-day rest God established at creation, codified at Sinai, transposed in the New Covenant to the Lord's Day, and pointing forward to the eternal rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9). It is rest from work, but not idleness — rest that is itself worship.
webster_summary: The day of rest appointed by God; the seventh day in Old Covenant Israel, the first day in New Covenant practice; pointing toward eternal rest.
webster_full: SABBATH, n. The day of rest; the day of the week which the Hebrews observed as a day of holy rest.

Three layers in Christian thinking: (1) the creation-pattern Sabbath of Genesis 2; (2) the Mosaic Sabbath of Exodus 20; (3) the Christian Lord's Day, the first day of the week, on which Christ rose. All three converge in the eschatological Sabbath of Hebrews 4:9 — the rest that remains.
scriptures: Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day.
corruption_summary: Two errors crowd Sabbath discussion: rigorism (no real rest, only rules) and laxity (no real day, only sentiment). Scripture commends a third path: real day, real rest.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's correction in Mark 2:27 strikes at rigorism: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath. The day is gift, not burden. Modern Christians often default to the opposite error: no real day, no real rest, just whatever lull happens.

Hebrews 4:9 keeps the rest open: there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. The household's Lord's Day is a foretaste of that rest — gathered worship, simple meals, deliberate cessation, eyes lifted forward to the eternal Sabbath.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabbat (to cease, rest) is the foundational verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabbat — to cease, rest; from the verb's seventh-day cessation in Genesis 2:2.
Greek katapausis — rest, the eschatological rest of Hebrews 4.
usage: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
The Lord's Day is a foretaste of the eternal Sabbath.
Rest is gift; do not refuse it.

etymology: Composite. The two-Genesis frame: work given as blessing in Eden (Gen 2:15), then cursed in its soil after the Fall (Gen 3:17-19).
biblical_def: Work is both cursed and blessed in Scripture: blessed as the original calling of Adam in unfallen creation (Gen 2:15); cursed in its soil and texture after the Fall (Gen 3:17-19). The redemption in Christ does not yet remove the curse from the soil but begins to redeem the worker; the new creation will fully restore the original blessing.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The biblical understanding of work as both originally blessed and post-Fall cursed; awaiting full redemption in Christ.
webster_full: Three frames stack: (1) Eden — work as unfallen vocation (Gen 2:15); (2) Fall — soil cursed, work soaked in sweat (Gen 3:17-19); (3) Christ — the worker redeemed, the soil not yet (Romans 8:20-22 awaits the cosmic redemption).
The saint's work today bears both stamps: the original dignity of pre-Fall calling and the present friction of post-Fall ground. Both are real.
scriptures: And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it.
Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Two errors: treating work as wholly cursed (so any rest from it is gospel) or wholly blessed (so any complaint about it is unspiritual). Scripture insists on both.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 2 and Genesis 3 must both be honored. Adam worked unfallen; he worked fallen. The curse is real (the soil resists, the body tires); the blessing is real (the calling was given before the Fall and is being restored in Christ).

1 Corinthians 15:58 is the redemption note: the saint's labor is not in vain in the Lord. The curse on the soil is temporary; the dignity of work, redeemed in Christ, is eternal. Work hard now; the new earth will be fully recovered.
roots_summary: Genesis 2 and Genesis 3 supply the dual framing.
roots_lines: Hebrew avad (Gen 2:15) — to work, serve; the unfallen vocation.
Hebrew itzavon (Gen 3:17) — sorrow, painful labor; the post-Fall texture.
usage: Genesis 2 and Genesis 3 must both be honored.
Work is blessed in calling, cursed in soil, redeemed in Christ.
Your labor is not in vain in the Lord — the redemption note.

etymology: Greek epiousios (sufficient for the coming day) plus artos (bread). Christ's petition for the day's sustenance.
biblical_def: Daily bread, in the Lord's Prayer, is the day's sufficient provision — not hoarded, not scarce, but given each day as needed. The Greek epiousios is rare and exact: bread for today, asked for today. The petition assumes the saint's daily work as the means and confesses the daily provision as the gift.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The day's sufficient provision; what the saint asks for in the Lord's Prayer and works for through honest labor.
webster_full: Greek epiousios appears only in Mt 6:11 and Lk 11:3 in all of Greek literature; its precise sense is debated but most likely sufficient for the coming day.
The petition presumes labor (the saint who would not work, would not eat — 2 Thess 3:10) and confesses dependence (no work guarantees the harvest). Both are right; both are kept in tension.
scriptures: Give us this day our daily bread.
Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me.
Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day.
If any would not work, neither should he eat.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often expects either no provision (anxiety) or guaranteed provision (presumption); Scripture teaches the saint to ask each day, work each day, eat each day.
corruption_paragraphs: The manna pattern in Exodus 16 is the original training in daily bread: gather each morning, do not hoard, expect God again tomorrow. The Lord's Prayer turns this into a daily petition: give us this day our daily bread.

Daily bread teaches a particular shape of stewardship: enough labor for today, enough provision for today, enough rest for today. The household that prays this prayer with conviction works diligently and worries less. Both halves are God's business.
roots_summary: Greek epiousios is the rare and exact word.
roots_lines: Greek epiousios — sufficient for the coming day; appears only in the Lord's Prayer.
Hebrew parallel: the manna of Exodus 16, gathered day by day.
usage: Give us this day our daily bread; not next year's.
Manna trained Israel in daily bread; the prayer trains the church.
Enough labor for today; enough provision for today; enough rest for today.

etymology: Latin capitalis, of the head; the principal sum of money or stock from which interest, return, or future labor flows.
biblical_def: Capital is accumulated stored value — money, tools, land, livestock, skill — that produces future return when wisely deployed. Scripture is unembarrassed about it: Abraham was rich in cattle, silver, and gold (Gen 13:2); Job had vast capital before and after his trial; Christ's parables of the talents and minas honor the servant who deployed the master's capital well. The question is never whether to have capital but how to steward it.
webster_summary: Wealth or stock employed for productive purposes; the principal sum that yields return.
webster_full: CAPITAL, n. The principal or main stock of a person or company employed in productive work; that part of one's wealth invested with a view to the production of further wealth.

Christ's parable of the talents (Mt 25:14-30) treats master-given capital as something the servant is morally bound to deploy for return. Burying it — the conservative-sounding option — is condemned as wickedness.
scriptures: Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.
Thou wicked and slothful servant... thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury.
And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold.
corruption_summary: Two opposite errors: capital is Mammon (so renounce all of it) or capital is virtue (so accumulate without restraint). Scripture teaches stewardship: deploy what you have for the Master's return.
corruption_paragraphs: The talents parable rebukes the servant who buried capital out of fear. Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers. Inactive capital is judged; deployed capital is rewarded. Christ's economic ethic in this parable is anything but anti-investment.

Yet 1 Timothy 6:9-10 warns the love of money. The line is the heart, not the size. The household with wisely deployed capital, given generously, recognized as the Master's, faithfully reported — that is the Matthew 25 pattern.
roots_summary: Greek talanton (talent) and mina are the parable's capital-units.
roots_lines: Greek talanton — talent, a large sum of money (~6,000 denarii); behind ‘talents’ in Mt 25.
Note: Christ's parable does not say everyone gets equal capital; it says everyone is judged by deployment of what was given.
usage: Inactive capital is judged; deployed capital is rewarded.
Occupy till I come — the Master's standing order.
The line is the heart, not the size.

etymology: Middle English slogarde, sluggish person; the chronically lazy man whom Proverbs warns against by name.
biblical_def: The sluggard is Proverbs' recurring antagonist: the chronically lazy man whose laziness has hardened into character. Proverbs catalogues his habits: he loves sleep, he turns on his bed as a door on its hinges, his vineyard is overgrown, his hand stays in his bowl, he says there is a lion in the way. He is the saint's living warning.
webster_summary: A person habitually lazy or inactive; a slothful man.
webster_full: SLUGGARD, n. A person habitually lazy, idle, and inactive; a drone.

Proverbs is the New Testament's and Old Testament's most concentrated treatment of the type: chapters 6, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 26 all contain sluggard sayings. The portrait is detailed and unsparing.
scriptures: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.
The slothful man saith, There is a lion without, I shall be slain in the streets.
As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often softens Proverbs' ridicule of the sluggard; Solomon does not. The portrait stays sharp.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs ridicules the sluggard with comic sharpness: as the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed. The man does not fall into laziness; he rotates in it. The image is funny precisely because it is true.
The household with this Proverb on the wall in season catches itself before it slides. The recovery is not heroic; it is the next chore done. Sluggards become diligent one undertaken task at a time.
roots_summary: Hebrew atzel (lazy, sluggard) is Proverbs' recurring noun.
roots_lines: Hebrew atzel — sluggard, lazy person; the Proverbs antagonist.
Note: Proverbs draws the ant as the sluggard's antithesis (Prov 6:6-8) — small, wise, self-disciplined.
usage: As the door on its hinges, so the sluggard on his bed.
Sluggards become diligent one undertaken task at a time.
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.

etymology: Old English bere-ærn (barley-house); the storage building for harvested grain and shelter for livestock.
biblical_def: A barn is the storage building for harvested grain. Scripture knows two: the wise barn that holds increase against future need (the patient farmer's ordinary tool) and the foolish barn that becomes the rich man's idol (Lk 12:18). Christ's harvest parable promises the wheat is gathered into His barn while the tares are burned.
webster_summary: A covered building for storing grain, hay, flax, and other produce of the earth, and for housing livestock.
webster_full: BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
Two famous biblical barn-passages: the rich fool's greater barns (Lk 12:18) and Christ's harvest barn into which the wheat is gathered (Mt 13:30; 3:12). Same word, opposite uses.
scriptures: Gather the wheat into my barn.
He will gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff.
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater.
Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often quotes Luke 12 against any saving and Matthew 13 against any judgment; both readings are flat. Scripture lets barns be both wise tool and idolatrous trap, depending on the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The rich fool's sin was not having barns; it was making them his salvation. Soul, take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry — the soul cannot rest in a barn, only in God. The barns themselves are morally neutral; the heart is the question.

Christ's eschatological barn (Mt 13:30) is the harvest's gathering point: the wheat is brought in. The household's daily barn rehearses it: store wisely, give generously, look forward to the great Harvest.
roots_summary: Hebrew asam (storehouse, granary) and Greek apothēkē (barn, storehouse) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Hebrew asam — storehouse, granary.
Greek apothēkē — barn, storehouse; same word in Mt 13:30 and Lk 12:18.
usage: The rich fool's sin was not the barn; it was the heart in it.
The wheat is gathered into His barn; the chaff is burned.
Store wisely; give generously; look forward to the Harvest.

etymology: Old French vigne (vine) plus Old English dressere (one who prepares). The skilled tender of grapevines — pruner, watcher, harvester.
biblical_def: A vinedresser is the skilled tender of grapevines — specifically, the one who prunes, props, and prepares the vines for fruit-bearing. Scripture calls the Father the husbandman (Jn 15:1) and reserves the title for the Spirit-led shepherd (Isa 61:5). The vinedresser's pruning shears are mentioned more often than his picking baskets — the work is more cutting than gathering.
webster_summary: One who dresses and tends vines; specifically, one who prunes them for fruit.
webster_full: VINEDRESSER, n. One whose business is to dress vines; one whose occupation is to trim, prune, and cultivate vines.

John 15's vinedresser is the Father, whose work is principally pruning — cutting away unfruitful branches and purging fruitful ones for greater fruit. The picture is sharper than the modern listener often hears.
scriptures: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant.
And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity flinches at the pruning shears; the vinedresser's work is principally cutting, not picking.
corruption_paragraphs: John 15 is uncomfortable in this respect: the Father's ordinary work toward His own bearing branches is to cut. Not punishment; pruning. The branch that is pruned bears more fruit precisely because of the cutting.

The pastor who refuses to prune his flock is no vinedresser. The household that resists pruning will not bear. The Father's shears are an act of love — received well, they multiply fruit; resisted, they leave the branch where it was.
roots_summary: Greek geōrgos (farmer, husbandman) and Hebrew korem (vinedresser) carry the title.
roots_lines: Greek geōrgos — farmer, husbandman; here the Father (Jn 15:1).
Hebrew korem — vinedresser; the skilled tender.
usage: The vinedresser's work is principally pruning.
Pruning is the ordinary love of the Father for the bearing branch.
Received well, the shears multiply fruit.

etymology: Old English ortgeard (yard for plants); a planted area of fruit-bearing trees.
biblical_def: An orchard is a planted area of fruit-bearing trees — the patient husbandman's long-term project. Scripture knows the orchard primarily as the picture of the saint's long fruitfulness: like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season. The orchard takes years to begin bearing and decades to peak; so does the saint.
webster_summary: An enclosure or yard containing a number of fruit trees; specifically, planted for crop.
webster_full: ORCHARD, n. An inclosure of fruit trees, generally a piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of fruits.
Old Testament Israel had olive groves, fig orchards, and pomegranate plantings; the Song of Solomon's orchard imagery (Song 4:13) carries the household-of-fruitfulness meaning into wedding poetry.
scriptures: And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season.
Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits.
For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river.
And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat... it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often expects fruit instantly; the orchard requires years of root-deep waiting before any harvest is taken.
corruption_paragraphs: An orchard is a generational gift. The man who plants apple trees may not eat from them; his grandchildren will. The household that thinks in orchard-time gives different gifts than the household that thinks in quarter-time.
Psalm 1's tree, Jeremiah 17's tree, Ezekiel 47's trees — all bring forth fruit in season. The off-seasons are real and necessary. The orchard mindset preserves the saint through the off-seasons.
roots_summary: Hebrew pardes (orchard, park) is the Song of Solomon's word.
roots_lines: Hebrew pardes — orchard, park; loanword from Persian, behind English paradise.
Note: paradise in the New Testament (Lk 23:43; 2 Cor 12:4; Rev 2:7) carries the same garden-orchard sense.
usage: An orchard is a generational gift.
The off-seasons are real and necessary.
Plant trees you may not eat from; your grandchildren will.

etymology: Old English dæg (day) plus Latin laborator. The hired worker paid by the day, often for harvest or construction.
biblical_def: A day laborer is a worker hired for the day — paid at sundown, expected to feed his family on what he earned that day. Scripture commands honest treatment of him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning (Lev 19:13). Christ's parable of the laborers in the vineyard (Mt 20) makes the day laborer a teacher of grace.
webster_summary: (Composite.) A worker hired and paid by the day; especially in agricultural or building work.
webster_full: LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation, especially with the hands; a manual workman.

The day laborer's economic vulnerability is foundational in biblical ethics: he is paid daily because he depends on the day's wage to feed his family that night. Withholding it overnight is a sin against him (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:15).
scriptures: The wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning.
At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it.
For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.
Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth.
corruption_summary: Modern wage-systems hide the day laborer from middle-class view; Scripture refuses the hiding and demands honest, prompt payment.
corruption_paragraphs: James 5:4 is one of the New Testament's sharpest economic verses: the hire of the labourers... which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth. The wages cry out; the Lord of hosts hears. Withheld pay is not a bookkeeping issue; it is a sin with a voice.

Christ's vineyard parable in Matthew 20 turns day-laborer economics into a parable of grace: the householder pays the eleventh-hour worker the same as the all-day worker. The first murmur; the householder rebukes them. The kingdom is generous, not transactional.
roots_summary: Greek misthios and ergatēs name the hired worker.
roots_lines: Greek misthios — hired servant, day laborer.
Greek ergatēs — worker, laborer; the ‘laborer’ of Mt 20:1 and Mt 9:37.
usage: Pay your laborer the day's wage by sundown.
Withheld pay has a voice; the Lord of hosts hears.
The kingdom is generous, not transactional.

etymology: Old French wage, pledge, payment; what is owed in exchange for labor.
biblical_def: Wage is what is owed the worker in exchange for labor — an obligation Scripture takes with the highest seriousness. Paul: the labourer is worthy of his reward (1 Tim 5:18). James: withheld wages cry out (5:4). Romans: to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt (Rom 4:4). Wage is debt owed; grace is gift given. The two must not be confused.
webster_summary: That which is paid for service rendered; salary; hire; the compensation for work.
webster_full: WAGES, n. plural. Hire; reward; compensation; especially payment for service rendered by labor.
Two New Testament uses converge: the literal wage owed the laborer (1 Tim 5:18; James 5:4) and the figurative wages of sin (Rom 6:23) — what sin pays its workers. Both are owed; neither is grace.
scriptures: For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
The labourer is worthy of his reward.
For the labourer is worthy of his hire.
Call the labourers, and give them their hire.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity sometimes confuses wage and grace; Scripture sharply distinguishes them.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 4:4 sets the doctrine: to the worker, the wage is reckoned of debt, not of grace. Romans 6:23 splits the lines: sin pays wages (death); God gives a gift (eternal life). The kingdom never confuses what is owed with what is given.

The household's practical payment of wages should match. Pay what is owed; pay it promptly; pay it generously. Then give gifts on top — gifts of grace, distinguishable from wages, expanding the scope of the household's witness.
roots_summary: Greek misthos (wage, reward) and Hebrew sakar (wage, hire) carry the term.
roots_lines: Greek misthos — wage, reward; what is paid for service.
Hebrew sakar — wage, hire, reward; the worker's due.
usage: Wage is debt; grace is gift; do not confuse them.
Pay what you owe promptly; pay it generously; then give gifts on top.
The wages of sin is death; the gift of God is eternal life.
